figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed CPDA methodology. Source and target time-series are mapped to latent temporal paths by a shared feature extractor. CPDA constructs pooled, temporal-path, spectral, and signature-based representations from these latent paths and evaluates a composite kernel. Source labels and target soft pseudo-labels provide class-conditional weights.
Table 2: Summary of notations used throughout the paper.
Table 3: Table 2 continued.
Table 4: Existing discrepancy losses as restricted cases of CPDA.
Table 5: Main CPDA hyperparameters used in the experiments and their default value.
Table 6: Summary of the backbone architectures used in the experiments. Architectural values are determined by the datasetspecific AdaTime (Ragab et al. 2023) configuration.
Table 7: Important configuration parameters used by the backbone implementations.

Table 8: Overview of datasets used in the evaluation. Sample counts refer to the total number of samples used in the corresponding standard train / test split or benchmark preprocessing. Datasets are available at https://researchdata.ntu.edu.sg/dataverse/ adatime, https://www.timeseriesclassification.com/dataset.php, or https://www.iis.fraunhofer.de/de/ff/lv/dataanalytics/anwproj/ schreibtrainer/onhw-dataset.html.

Table 9: Results for the source and target test datasets, which are evaluated on the model trained solely on target samples to show the discrepancy between source and target domains. For all datasets, we report the accuracy and F1-score in % for the CNN, ResNet18, and TCN encoder networks. These metrics are averaged over all domain scenarios and five training runs. Bold refers to the best-performing encoder network on target and source accuracy.
Table 10: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the HHAR (Stisen et al. 2015) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 11: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the UCI HAR (Anguita et al. 2013) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 12: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the WISDM (Kwapisz, Weiss, and Moore 2010) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 13: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the EEG (Goldberger et al. 2000) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 14: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the uWave (Liu et al. 2009) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 15: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the PenDigits (Alimoglu and Alpaydin 1997) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 16: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the Epilepsy (Villar et al. 2016) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 17: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the Face detection (Olivetti, Kia, and Avesani 2014) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 18: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the Finger movements (Blankertz, Curio, and Müller 2001) dataset. Bold are best results.
Table 19: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the Gestures mid air (Caputo et al. 2018) dataset. Bold are best results.

Table 20: DA results in % (mean and standard deviation over all scenarios and five runs) for the OnHW-symbols, split OnHWequations, and OnHW-chars (Ott et al. 2020, 2022b) datasets. CNN backbone as encoder network. Bold are best results.
Figure 4: Comparison of the recent DA methods on the OnHW datasets for the adaptation from left- to right-handed writers (L → R) and the adaptation from right- to left-handed writers (R → L).
Figure 7: Evaluation results of a large collection of source–target DA pairs for each dataset. The dashed lines show average results over all source–target combinations.
